Sampling of regions near fracture surfaces

analytical_models.equation_role: Relate XRD peak broadening to crystallite size D and lattice strain ε
analytical_models.model_note: (Δ2θ cosθ)/λ = 0.9/D + 2ε sinθ/λ; fitted to the (110)M, (200)M and (211) M diffraction peaks

analytical_models.equation_role: Calculate dislocation density from lattice strain and crystallite size

computational_details.simulation_method: Williamson-Hall analysis of XRD peak broadening
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Dislocation density estimated as ~2.20 × 10^15 m^-2 for the 1.3Al steel (vs ~2.01 × 10^15 m^-2 for 0Al), consistent with EBSD KAM analysis

defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Ultrafine, densely distributed NiAl clusters hinder dislocation motion by increasing cluster density and reducing dislocation mean free path; clusters are sheared by mobile dislocations, promoting uniform dislocation structures, suppressing pile-ups at boundaries and mitigating local stress concentration near the main crack.

defect_interactions.interaction_type: Si segregation / heterogeneous nucleation of NiAl
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: A fraction of NiAl clusters preferentially precipitates along Si- and Cr-enriched banded zones; Si rises from 4.21 at.% in the matrix to 11.21 at.% (Cr from 1.65 to 5.83 at.%, Mo from 0.33 to 1.35 at.%), providing favourable heterogeneous nucleation sites and slightly larger (still nanoscale) clusters.
ε-carbides promote dislocation cell formation through bypassing, whereas closely spaced NiAl clusters are directly sheared; the refined dislocation network suppresses localized strain accumulation.

interfaces.interface_notes: The main crack propagates transgranularly, cutting across packets and deflecting at block boundaries (prior austenite grain boundaries 15° ≤ θ < 50° in yellow, packet/block boundaries θ ≥ 50° in blue).
interfaces.phase_evolution: During low-temperature tempering at 180 °C, ε-carbides and NiAl clusters nucleate and grow independently, with no observable elemental overlap or competitive partitioning between C and Ni/Al; NiAl clusters remain in early nucleation stages (cluster-centre Ni/Al ~13 at.%, below stoichiometric NiAl).

phase_interfaces.coherence: fully coherent; no discernible interface between NiAl and matrix; lattice mismatch ~0.5 % (NiAl ~2.882 nm vs matrix ~2.866 nm)

interfaces.slip_behavior: NiAl clusters are sheared by mobile dislocations; ε-carbides are bypassed by dislocations. The dense NiAl cluster dispersion increases lattice friction and produces a more uniform dislocation structure (uniform KAM distribution) enabling coordinated deformation.

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: impact absorption energy KU2, fracture toughness KIC, crack-initiation energy Ei, crack-propagation energy Ep
comparative_performance.improvement_percentage: KU2 rose from 23 ± 2 J (as-quenched) to ~80 ± 3 J (~3.5 times); vs 0Al,2 h the 1.3Al,2 h steel had ~23 % higher impact absorption energy; KIC 108.0 vs 97.6 MPa·m^1/2 (10.4 MPa·m^1/2 higher); Ei 37.8 % higher; Ep 20.7 % higher

processing_steps.method: vacuum induction melting followed by vacuum arc remelting (VIM + VAR)
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Both materials were produced by VIM + VAR to obtain 500 kg ingots.
Ingots were subsequently forged into billets with Φ170 mm; specimens extracted from quarter-radius position.
Solution treatment to dissolve carbides, with water quenching after the step; the resulting state is the as-quenched (WQ) condition.
Low-temperature tempering at 180 °C for 2 h with water quenching; this defines the 1.3Al,2 h (tempered) state of the present sample.

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Engineering stress-strain curve for 1.3Al, 2h (dashed magenta) peaking near 1900–1950 MPa at strain ~8–9 and extending to strain ~14, ending near 1250–1300 MPa (Fig. 1a).

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: three-point bending specimens, thickness 25 mm, width 50 mm, with a 3 mm fatigue pre-crack at the notch tip

defects.lattice_distortion: average KAM 1.31° near fracture surface; matrix KAM 0.79°

phases_present.morphology: tempered martensitic laths/plates with sharp boundaries
thin films at lath boundaries; Kurdjumov-Sachs orientation relationship with martensite {111}γ//{110}M, <110>γ//<111>M

phases_present.grain_size: length 100–500 nm, width 3–10 nm (also reported as ~100–500 nm length and 2–4 nm thickness; APT average thickness ~2.2 nm, spacing ~10 nm)

near-spherical clusters, remarkably uniformly distributed within the matrix

size.value: length 100–500 nm, width 3–10 nm (APT ~2.2 nm thickness, ~10 nm spacing)

precipitates.coherency: fully coherent with the martensitic matrix (no discernible interface; lattice mismatch ~0.5 %)
precipitates.distribution: number density 4.88 × 10^24 m^-3; remarkably uniformly distributed; a fraction precipitates along Si- and Cr-enriched banded zones as clusters <5 nm; slight segregation of Si, Mo and Cr within the clusters

structures.overall_structure: Tempered martensitic lath structure (lath-shaped tempered martensite with sharp lath boundaries and high dislocation density) containing thin retained-austenite films at lath boundaries, needle-like ε-carbides precipitated uniformly within the laths, and extremely high-density near-spherical NiAl clusters uniformly dispersed in the matrix.

unmapped_findings: Instrumented Charpy U-notch impact data for the 1.3Al,2 h steel (Fig. 7c): peak load P_m = 38.6 KN, crack-initiation energy E_i = 62.0 J, crack-propagation energy E_p = 21.0 J, and total KU2 = 83.0 J; impact toughness from the bar chart is 80 ± 3 J.

Charpy U-notch impact toughness KU2 of the 1.3Al,2 h steel was measured as approximately 80 ± 3 J, corresponding to an improvement of about 3.5 times compared to its as-quenched state (23 ± 2 J); this is ~23 % higher impact absorption energy than the 0Al,2 h steel.

Peak loads (P_M) for the 1.3Al steel occurred at a deflection of 2.55 mm, with crack propagation accelerating at ~3 mm; rapid fracture occurred near the specimen center without an obvious crack-arrest stage.

Impact fracture of the 1.3Al,2 h steel showed a shear fracture area of 42.9 % (vs 36.8 % for 0Al), with enhanced number and size of large/deep primary dimples, more prominent tearing ridges and greater overall surface roughness, indicating ductile void growth and coalescence combined with quasi-cleavage.

In the 1.3Al steel, secondary cracks and voids measuring 5–10 μm were observed 8–18 μm below the main crack in fracture-toughness specimens, interconnected by fine cracks coalescing into larger secondary cracks; crack paths showed frequent deflections.

EBSD KAM of the 1.3Al steel near the impact fracture surface averaged 1.31° (matrix value 0.79°, Fig. S5), with a uniform distribution indicating homogeneous strain distribution; the 0Al steel showed 1.16° with inhomogeneous red/yellow patches near the crack.

Retained austenite content of the 1.3Al,2 h steel is 1.8 % (0.8 % higher than the 0Al steel); the toughness improvement is attributed mainly to NiAl cluster dispersion rather than the retained-austenite increase.

NiAl cluster lattice parameter (~2.882 nm) closely matches the martensitic matrix (~2.866 nm), giving a lattice mismatch of only ~0.5 %; Mo and Cr atoms expand the matrix lattice and further reduce the mismatch, lowering the nucleation barrier.

The abstract reports the 1.3Al steel overall exhibits an ultimate tensile strength of ~1.9 GPa, total elongation ~15 %, U-notch impact absorption energy ~80 J and a fracture toughness of 108 MPa·m^1/2.
